To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the homoconjugation of acetic acid and phenols, and of amines with imidazoles and 4(6)‐methyl imidazoles is a thermodynamically favored process.

the homoconjugation equilibria in the systems studied were found to be strongly dependent on the solvent polarity and hydrogen‐binding propensity and that the homoconjunction equilibria were found to be more favorable than the heteroconjugation equilibrums in systems modeling the interactions of amino acids and their side chains with the environment.

the homoconjugation of acetic acid and phenolic compounds is more favorable in nonpolar and aprotic solvents (acetonitrile) than in polar and protic ones (dimethyl sulfoxide, water), and that homoconjugation equilibria are shifted towards the homoconjugated forms in solutions of higher polarity and hydrogen‐binding propensity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the theoretical calculations of homocongugation equilibriums constants for systems modeling acid–bases interactions in side chains in biomolecules.
the study of homoconjugate equilibria in solution.
the theoretical modeling of homoconjugated acid‐base systems in solution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the calculated homoconjugations equilibrium constants are in good qualitative and in most cases quantitative agreement with the experimental data.
, in the systems considered in this study, homoconjugate interactions are more favorable than heteroconjugate interactions.

the calculated equilibrium constants for the homoconjugation reactions of acetic acid and phenolic systems are in agreement with the experiment, while the calculated constants for imidazole are too low, and for n‐butyl and isopropyl amine are too high.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed and validated a method for calculating homoconjugation equilibria of biomolecules in solution and applied it to a number of model systems.
we have shown how to use the potential of mean forces (PMFs) for calculation of homoconjugate constants.
the PMFs calculated by using the AMBER force‐field are in good agreement with the experimental data and that they are useful tools in the study of the homoconjugation in solution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to use the potential of mean forces (PMFs) to estimate homoconjugation (HC) constants for the model systems.
the PMFs calculated with the umbrella sampling method are a useful tool for the study of homoconjugated complexes in solution, which can provide a basis for the interpretation of experimental data.
we have shown how to compute the equilibrium constant for a homoconjugation reaction from a potential of mean force (a free energy profile) using the weighted histogram analysis method.
